spec.title: Artificial Intelligence: What It Is, How It Began and How It Works
spec.subtitle: A research brief with material for a timeline, a subfield hierarchy, a machine learning diagram and an image sourcing guide

sections.heading: What Is Artificial Intelligence?
sections.notes: This brief draws on well-established history and definitions. It does not cite live web sources, and none were fetched to write it.

blocks.text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is the field of computer science that builds systems able to do tasks that normally need human intelligence. These tasks include perceiving the world, understanding language, reasoning, learning from experience, planning and making decisions. John McCarthy, who coined the term, defined it as "the science and engineering of making intelligent machines."

There are two broad ways to define AI. One focuses on behaviour: does the system act intelligently? The other focuses on process: does it reason the way a mind does? Most modern AI is engineering-driven. It aims to perform useful tasks well, not to copy human thought exactly.

items: Narrow (weak) AI: systems built for a specific task, such as translation, image recognition or playing chess. All AI deployed today is narrow in this sense, although modern large models cover a very wide range of tasks.
Artificial general intelligence (AGI): a hypothetical system that could match human ability across almost any intellectual task. Its definition and timeline are still debated.
Superintelligence: a speculative system that would exceed human ability in nearly every domain.
Symbolic AI: intelligence built from explicit rules, logic and symbols written by people.
Connectionist (statistical) AI: intelligence that emerges from networks and models learning patterns from data. This is the approach behind today's machine learning.

blocks.text: The idea of artificial minds is much older than computers. Greek myth described Talos, a bronze automaton. Medieval and early modern thinkers such as Ramon Llull and Gottfried Leibniz imagined mechanical reasoning. In 1843, Ada Lovelace wrote about Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine and considered whether machines could go beyond calculating. AI as a scientific field only became possible once programmable electronic computers existed in the 1940s.

The field's history has swung between optimism and disappointment. There were bursts of progress and funding, followed by "AI winters" when results fell short of promises. Three things drove the modern boom from the 2010s onward: large datasets, powerful GPUs and better neural network methods.

sections.heading: Key Milestones Timeline
sections.notes: Suggested timeline diagram: plot each row as a node on a horizontal axis and colour-code the eras (Foundations, Early Enthusiasm, First Winter, Expert Systems, Second Winter, Statistical ML, Deep Learning, Generative AI). The table stops at 2024. Check later developments against current sources before publishing.

rows: McCulloch and Pitts publish a mathematical model of the neuron
The first formal model of an artificial neural network
Alan Turing publishes "Computing Machinery and Intelligence"
Proposed the imitation game (Turing Test) as a test of machine intelligence
Minsky's SNARC and Strachey's checkers program
Among the earliest neural network machines and game-playing programs
Dartmouth Summer Research Project on AI
The founding event of AI as a field. The term "artificial intelligence" comes from the 1955 proposal by McCarthy, Minsky, Rochester and Shannon
Logic Theorist (Newell, Simon and Shaw)
Often called the first AI program. It proved mathematical theorems
Rosenblatt's Perceptron; McCarthy creates LISP
The first trainable neural network, plus a dominant AI programming language
Arthur Samuel popularises the term "machine learning"
His checkers program improved by playing against itself
ELIZA chatbot (Joseph Weizenbaum)
An early natural-language program that simulated conversation
Minsky and Papert publish "Perceptrons"
Showed the limits of single-layer networks and helped slow neural network research
Lighthill Report and the first AI winter
Funding cuts after progress fell short of expectations
Expert systems boom (for example, XCON); Japan's Fifth Generation project
Rule-based AI saw commercial use
Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams popularise backpropagation
Made it practical to train multi-layer neural networks
Second AI winter
The Lisp machine market collapsed and interest in expert systems faded
IBM Deep Blue defeats Garry Kasparov at chess
A landmark public demonstration of machine performance
LeNet-5 convolutional network (Yann LeCun)
Practical handwritten-digit recognition and a template for computer vision
ImageNet dataset released
A large labelled dataset that drove progress in vision
IBM Watson wins Jeopardy!; Apple launches Siri
AI in question answering and consumer products
AlexNet wins the ImageNet competition
Started the deep learning revolution using GPUs
Generative adversarial networks (Ian Goodfellow)
A major step for generative models
DeepMind's AlphaGo defeats Lee Sedol 4–1 at Go
Deep learning combined with reinforcement learning mastered a very complex game
"Attention Is All You Need" introduces the Transformer
The architecture behind modern large language models
BERT and GPT-1; Hinton, LeCun and Bengio receive the Turing Award
Pre-trained language models took off, and deep learning received formal recognition
GPT-3; AlphaFold 2 at CASP14
Large-scale language models and a breakthrough in predicting protein structure
Image diffusion models (DALL-E 2, Stable Diffusion); ChatGPT released
Generative AI reached mass public use
GPT-4 and other multimodal models
Models handling text and images with stronger reasoning
EU AI Act enters into force; Nobel Prizes to Hopfield and Hinton (Physics) and to Hassabis and Jumper, shared with Baker (Chemistry)
The first comprehensive AI law, and Nobel-level recognition for AI research

sections.heading: AI Subfields Hierarchy
sections.notes: Suggested hierarchy diagram: use nested circles (AI, then Machine Learning, then Neural Networks, then Deep Learning, then Generative AI and LLMs), with the other branches drawn as siblings beside Machine Learning.

blocks.text: AI is best pictured as nested fields with branches off to the side. Machine learning is a subset of AI. Deep learning is a subset of machine learning. Generative AI and large language models (LLMs) are one application of deep learning. Some areas are methods (such as search or learning). Others are application domains (such as vision or language) that use several methods.

Artificial Intelligence
├── Symbolic AI (Good Old-Fashioned AI)
│   ├── Knowledge representation and reasoning
│   ├── Logic and automated theorem proving
│   └── Expert systems
├── Search and Planning
│   ├── Heuristic search (e.g., A*)
│   ├── Game playing (e.g., minimax)
│   └── Automated planning and scheduling
├── Machine Learning
│   ├── Supervised learning
│   ├── Unsupervised learning
│   ├── Reinforcement learning
│   └── Neural Networks
│       └── Deep Learning
│           ├── Convolutional networks (vision)
│           ├── Recurrent networks (sequences)
│           ├── Transformers
│           └── Generative AI
│               ├── Large language models
│               └── Diffusion and image generation models
├── Application Domains
│   ├── Natural language processing
│   ├── Computer vision
│   ├── Speech recognition and synthesis
│   └── Robotics
└── Cross-cutting Concerns
    ├── AI safety and alignment
    └── Ethics, fairness and governance

sections.heading: How Machine Learning Works
sections.notes: Suggested flow diagram: show the numbered steps as boxes in a loop. Draw an arrow from 'Evaluate' back to 'Train' for iteration, and one from 'Monitor' back to 'Collect data' for retraining.

blocks.text: Traditional programming starts with rules and data and produces answers. Machine learning turns this around. It starts with data and example answers, and the algorithm learns the rules, in the form of a model with adjustable parameters. Training means repeatedly adjusting those parameters to reduce the gap between the model's predictions and the correct answers.

items: Define the problem: what should be predicted or decided (for example, spam or not spam).
Collect data: gather examples relevant to the task.
Prepare data: clean it, label it and turn it into features, then split it into training, validation and test sets.
Choose a model: for example linear regression, decision trees or neural networks.

Train: the model makes predictions, a loss function measures the error, and an optimiser (usually gradient descent, with backpropagation for neural networks) adjusts the parameters to reduce that error.
Evaluate: measure performance on held-out data to check that the model generalises and has not just memorised the training set.
Tune: adjust hyperparameters, features or architecture and retrain.
Deploy: use the model to make predictions on new, real-world data (inference).
Monitor: track performance over time and retrain when the data drifts.

rows: Supervised
Labelled input–output pairs
Learn to map inputs to known outputs
Spam filtering, image classification, price prediction
Unsupervised
Unlabelled data
Find structure or patterns
Customer segmentation, anomaly detection
Self-supervised
Unlabelled data that creates its own targets
Learn general representations
Next-word prediction for pre-training LLMs
Reinforcement
Rewards from interacting with an environment
Learn actions that maximise long-term reward
AlphaGo, robot control, game agents
Algorithm
A step-by-step procedure for solving a problem or learning from data
Model
The learned mathematical function that makes predictions
Parameters (weights)
Internal values the model adjusts during training
Training data
Examples the model learns from
Feature
A measurable input property used by a model
Loss function
A measure of how wrong the model's predictions are
Gradient descent
An optimisation method that lowers the loss step by step
Backpropagation
The method for computing the gradients that update each weight in a neural network
Neural network
Layers of connected artificial neurons that transform inputs into outputs
Deep learning
Neural networks with many layers that learn layered representations
Overfitting
Memorising the training data instead of learning patterns that generalise
Inference
Using a trained model to make predictions on new data
Transformer
A neural architecture based on attention, used in modern LLMs
Large language model
A transformer trained on huge amounts of text to predict and generate language
Bias (in AI)
Systematic unfair outcomes, often inherited from training data
Alignment
Making sure AI systems act in line with human intentions and values

blocks.text: The table suggests images for each diagram and topic, with trustworthy places to search.
